note: Source registry. confidence: high = primary text, official body, or a titled-player publication; medium = recognised educator or established site with named authorship; low = unsourced blog, forum, AI-written or anonymous page. Record low-confidence sources rather than discarding them, so a claim's provenance stays auditable.

nimzowitsch-my-system.title: My System (Mein System)
nimzowitsch-my-system.author: Aron Nimzowitsch
nimzowitsch-my-system.note: Full text consulted directly. The relevant chapter is 'Manoeuvring' (Ch. 5/VI; Ch. 14 in the New in Chess edition), sections 1-3.

shereshevsky-endgame-strategy.title: Endgame Strategy (Revised & Expanded)
shereshevsky-endgame-strategy.author: Mikhail Shereshevsky
shereshevsky-endgame-strategy.note: Full text consulted directly. Source of the four endgame principles and, importantly, of the author's own documented counter-finding about rook endings. The original edition dates from 1985; this is the revised and expanded New in Chess edition.

dvoretsky-endgame-manual.title: Dvoretsky's Endgame Manual (5th edition), knight and queen endgame chapters
dvoretsky-endgame-manual.author: Mark Dvoretsky, revised by Karsten Mueller
dvoretsky-endgame-manual.note: Extract consulted directly. Source of Botvinnik's Formula as Dvoretsky states it, the deflecting knight sacrifice, the judgement that knight-versus-knight-and-pawn theory has no operative principles, and the modern downgrade of Fine's 1941 four-versus-three verdict.

dvoretsky-technique-in-chess.title: Technique in Chess
dvoretsky-technique-in-chess.author: Mark Dvoretsky / Artur Yusupov
dvoretsky-technique-in-chess.note: Publisher PDF. Lists 'The Principle of Two Weaknesses' as one of four golden principles of technique; contains the Kotov-Pachman analysis.

dvoretsky-shereshevsky-interview.title: Dvoretsky on the origin of Endgame Strategy (in 'Chess Family Belavenets')
dvoretsky-shereshevsky-interview.author: Mark Dvoretsky (interview)
dvoretsky-shereshevsky-interview.note: Dvoretsky describes his 'General Principles of Endgame Play' notebook and credits Belavenets as his own starting point. Key evidence for the Belavenets -> Dvoretsky -> Shereshevsky transmission.

fishbein-my-system-interview.title: My System (Fast Track Edition) — Q&A with editor GM Alex Fishbein
fishbein-my-system-interview.author: Alex Fishbein
fishbein-my-system-interview.note: Fishbein states he retitled Nimzowitsch's 'changing tack' chapter to 'playing against two weaknesses' because 'that is basically what it is'. Editorial testimony, not a primary text.

chesscom-ipatov-two-weaknesses.title: Principle of Two Weaknesses
chesscom-ipatov-two-weaknesses.author: GM Alexander Ipatov
chesscom-ipatov-two-weaknesses.note: Titled-player authorship; instructional rather than scholarly.

chesscom-smith-endgame-strategy.title: 'Endgame Strategy' by Mikhail Shereshevsky
chesscom-smith-endgame-strategy.author: GM Bryan Smith
chesscom-smith-endgame-strategy.note: Annotates Benko-Parma, Belgrade 1964 from the two-weaknesses chapter.

thechessworld-two-weaknesses.title: The Principle of Two Weaknesses
thechessworld-two-weaknesses.author: WGM Raluca Sgircea, IM Renier Castellanos
thechessworld-two-weaknesses.note: Repeats the Nimzowitsch attribution without citing a passage.

britishchessnews-kotov-pachman.title: Training: Kotov-Pachman, Venice 1950
britishchessnews-kotov-pachman.author: Richard James
britishchessnews-kotov-pachman.note: Engine-checked annotation of the full Kotov-Pachman ending.

chessskill-lasker-capablanca-g10.title: Lasker -- Capablanca, Game 10 (three-part annotation)
chessskill-lasker-capablanca-g10.author: James Stripes
chessskill-lasker-capablanca-g10.note: Valuable mainly as a carrier of primary annotations: quotes Capablanca (1921 match book and A Primer of Chess, 1935), Lasker, Shereshevsky, Kasparov, Lakdawala and Myers with page references.

chessterra-lasker-capablanca-g10.title: Lasker vs Capablanca, WCC Game 10 (1921) — full game score
chessterra-lasker-capablanca-g10.author: N. Haselton
chessterra-lasker-capablanca-g10.note: Used only for the move list, which was replayed and checked for legality.

wikipedia-fortress.title: Fortress (chess)
wikipedia-fortress.author: Wikipedia contributors
wikipedia-fortress.note: Distinguishes the elementary fortress (a book draw held by passive defence) from the general drawing technique, and relates both to the positional draw.

qualitymag-two-weaknesses.title: Principle of Two Weaknesses
qualitymag-two-weaknesses.author: Darryl Seland
qualitymag-two-weaknesses.note: Trade-magazine business analogy. Recorded only because it is a visible vector for the unsourced 'Nimzowitsch 1925' attribution.

fide-laws-2023.title: FIDE Laws of Chess, in force from 1 January 2023 (FIDE Handbook E.I.01)
fide-laws-2023.author: Fédération Internationale des Échecs
fide-laws-2023.note: Adopted at the 93rd FIDE Congress, Chennai. The English text is the authentic version. Full text retrieved and stored at research/fide-laws-2023.md. CAUTION: https://fide.com/FIDE/handbook/LawsOfChess.pdf still ranks highly in search engines and is a SUPERSEDED (2014/2018) edition — do not cite it.

fide-laws-2023-pdf.title: FIDE Laws of Chess (PDF, applied from 01/01/2023)
fide-laws-2023-pdf.author: FIDE Rules Commission
fide-laws-2023-pdf.note: PDF of the same authentic text; used as an independent copy to cross-check wording.

informant-encyclopedia-combinations.title: Encyclopaedia of Chess Combinations
informant-encyclopedia-combinations.author: Chess Informant (A. Matanović, ed.)
informant-encyclopedia-combinations.note: Benchmark reference work; classifies 3198 combinations under ten themes: a Annihilation of Defence, b Blockade, c Clearance, d Deflection, e Discovered Attack, f Pinning, g Demolition of Pawn structure, h Decoy, i Interference, j Double Attack. ACCESS CAVEAT: the theme list was read from the publisher's product description, not from the book itself. It is corroborated independently by Wikipedia's citation of the companion Encyclopedia of Chess Middlegames, whose category list overlaps and extends it. Treat the LIST as high confidence and any wording attributed to the book as unverified.

wikipedia-chess-tactic.title: Chess tactic
wikipedia-chess-tactic.author: Wikipedia contributors
wikipedia-chess-tactic.note: Cites the Encyclopedia of Chess Middlegames categories: Annihilation of Defense, Blockade, Decoying, Deflection, Demolition of Pawns, Discovered Attack, Double Attack, Interception, Intermediate Move, Overloading, Passed Pawn, Pawns Breakthrough, Pin, Pursuit (perpetual attack), Space Clearance, Trapping a piece, X-ray Attack.

chesstempo-tactical-motifs.title: Tactical Motifs and Themes
chesstempo-tactical-motifs.author: Chess Tempo
chesstempo-tactical-motifs.note: A working tagging taxonomy applied to a large tactics database. Useful evidence of which distinctions are operationally maintained (e.g. it separates X-Ray Attack from X-Ray Defense, and Relative from Absolute pins) rather than of historical usage.

steinitz-modern-chess-instructor.title: The Modern Chess Instructor, Part I
steinitz-modern-chess-instructor.author: Wilhelm Steinitz
steinitz-modern-chess-instructor.note: Chapter 7, 'Relative Value of Pieces and Principles of Play', p. xxxix, is where Steinitz defines the 'hole' and claims he coined it in The International Chess Magazine, November 1886. ACCESS CAVEAT: read via Mark Weeks' verbatim transcription, not the book. Wording corroborated independently by Edward Winter and Britannica.

mark-weeks-steinitz.title: Relative Value of Pieces and Principles of Play (Steinitz transcription)
mark-weeks-steinitz.author: Mark Weeks
mark-weeks-steinitz.note: Transcription vehicle for the Steinitz primary text; cited alongside it, not instead of it.

winter-chess-notes-steinitz.title: Steinitz, Lasker, Potter and 'Modern Chess' (Chess Notes)
winter-chess-notes-steinitz.author: Edward Winter
winter-chess-notes-steinitz.note: Winter is the standard authority on chess-historical attribution and is notably sceptical of received claims. On the 'hole' he records Lasker's attribution to Steinitz (Lasker's Manual, p.203) and Steinitz's own claim, while cautioning 'This one item is certainly not enough to settle the matter.' That caution is reproduced in the concept record rather than discarded.

oxford-companion-chess.title: The Oxford Companion to Chess (2nd ed.)
oxford-companion-chess.author: David Hooper and Kenneth Whyld
oxford-companion-chess.note: Standard reference. Defines outpost (p.285) as a square 'guarded by a pawn but cannot be attacked by an enemy pawn, especially such a square on an open file', and hole (p.175) as 'a square on a player's third rank or beyond that cannot be guarded by a pawn'. ACCESS CAVEAT: definitions quoted via two independent secondary sources (Wikipedia and the Chess Skills blog), not read from the book.

chessbase-india-bedouin-outpost.title: What is the definition of 'Outposts'? — a nomenclature
chessbase-india-bedouin-outpost.author: IM Xavier Bedouin
chessbase-india-bedouin-outpost.note: Titled-player proposal that exists BECAUSE the term is used inconsistently: 'the problem goes back to Nimzowitsch himself. In My System he suggests various examples, but he doesn't give clear definitions.' Distinguishes strong square, protected strong square, foothold (open file), and outpost (semi-open file), each absolute or relative. Recorded as a proposed refinement, NOT as established usage.

chessprogramming-outposts.title: Outposts
chessprogramming-outposts.author: Chess Programming Wiki contributors
chessprogramming-outposts.note: Useful because it states the drift explicitly: engine evaluation terms use the broad modern sense, in which 'the half-open file and provocation aspect of the outpost is lost, though the evaluation term is still useful.'

chesscom-outpost.title: Outpost (Chess Terms)
chesscom-outpost.author: Chess.com
chesscom-outpost.note: Gives the three modern conditions, including the often-omitted third: no piece of equal value can easily challenge the occupant.

wikipedia-outpost.title: Outpost (chess)
wikipedia-outpost.author: Wikipedia contributors
wikipedia-outpost.note: Follows Hooper & Whyld. Records Nimzowitsch's point that a flank outpost suits a rook rather than a knight.

romanovsky-middlegame-planning.title: Chess Middlegame Planning
romanovsky-middlegame-planning.author: Peter Romanovsky
romanovsky-middlegame-planning.note: Source of the 'eternal knight' refinement: a square is only a REAL weakness when a piece that cannot be driven away or exchanged threatens to occupy it. ACCESS CAVEAT: quoted via the Chess Skills blog, not read directly.

chessskill-outpost.title: Outpost
chessskill-outpost.author: James Stripes
chessskill-outpost.note: Valuable as a carrier of primary quotations: Nimzowitsch, Hooper & Whyld, Romanovsky and Steinitz with page references.

britannica-chess-theory.title: The Evolution of Chess Theory
britannica-chess-theory.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
britannica-chess-theory.note: Independent corroboration that Steinitz originated the term 'hole'.

nunn-secrets-practical-chess.title: Secrets of Practical Chess
nunn-secrets-practical-chess.author: John Nunn
nunn-secrets-practical-chess.note: The principal critique of Kotov's tree. Known through the Chessable research paper's detailed summary and Leitao's account, not read directly.

chessbase-lpdo.title: Loose Pieces Drop Off (LPDO)
chessbase-lpdo.author: ChessBase
chessbase-lpdo.note: States the acronym was 'probably coined by the English player Mike Cook' and popularised by Nunn. Note the hedge — it is reproduced rather than dropped. The comment thread also contains a substantive criticism that the article's own diagram is not an LPDO example but an instance of Lasker's geometric principle, which is kept as a counterexample.

chessworld-lpdo.title: What Does LPDO Mean in Chess?
chessworld-lpdo.author: Tryfon Gavriel
chessworld-lpdo.note: Independent attestation of the Cook/Nunn attribution, and of the loose-vs-hanging distinction.

chessbio-hanging.title: Hanging in Chess: Definition and Examples
chessbio-hanging.note: Sets out the three-way en prise / loose / hanging distinction explicitly. Low confidence (anonymous), used only for terminology corroboration.

chessmind-en-prise.title: En Prise / Hanging Piece / Weak Square (chess terms)
chessmind-en-prise.author: ChessMind AI
chessmind-en-prise.note: AI-authored site. Recorded because its terminology matches better sources and it articulates the loose-as-tactical-fuel progression clearly, NOT as an authority. Any claim resting on it alone must be marked low confidence.

chesscom-mastering-squares.title: Mastering Squares, Part 3
chesscom-mastering-squares.author: Chess.com
chesscom-mastering-squares.note: Records 'support point' as a further synonym for a usable weak square.

chessworld-weaknesses-outposts.title: Chess Weaknesses and Outposts
chessworld-weaknesses-outposts.author: Tryfon Gavriel
chessworld-weaknesses-outposts.note: Clean articulation of the hierarchy: 'A hole is the weak square itself, while an outpost is that square once a piece occupies it securely and uses it well.'

spielmann-art-of-sacrifice.title: The Art of Sacrifice in Chess
spielmann-art-of-sacrifice.author: Rudolf Spielmann
spielmann-art-of-sacrifice.publisher: originally Stahlberg; modern ed. Russell Enterprises
spielmann-art-of-sacrifice.note: The book that first tried to classify sacrifices systematically. Publisher teaser PDF consulted directly, containing Spielmann's own text on the sham/real division, the active/passive division, and the three classes of sham sacrifice. Later chapters (the real-sacrifice subdivisions) are known only through secondary summaries.

wikipedia-sacrifice.title: Sacrifice (chess)
wikipedia-sacrifice.author: Wikipedia contributors
wikipedia-sacrifice.note: Follows Spielmann's division and adds the forced/non-forced axis and the mechanism sub-types (deflection, destruction, magnet, clearance, tempo, suicide).

wikipedia-perpetual-check.title: Perpetual check
wikipedia-perpetual-check.author: Wikipedia contributors
wikipedia-perpetual-check.note: Load-bearing statement: 'A draw by perpetual check is no longer one of the rules of chess, but will eventually allow a draw claim by either threefold repetition or the fifty-move rule.' Also records that shogi and xiangqi forbid it outright, which is evidence that its status is a rules choice rather than a necessity.

thechessworld-positional-sacrifice.title: Positional Sacrifice: Complete Guide
thechessworld-positional-sacrifice.author: WGM Raluca Sgircea, IM Renier Castellanos
thechessworld-positional-sacrifice.note: Titled-player authorship. Emphasises Petrosian and the defensive positional sacrifice, which most treatments omit.

chesscom-real-vs-sham.title: Real vs. Sham Sacrifices in Chess, Part 1
chesscom-real-vs-sham.author: Jordan Hegel
chesscom-real-vs-sham.note: Amateur blog. Used only to corroborate Spielmann's category names, which it lists consistently with the primary text.

vukovic-art-of-attack.title: The Art of Attack in Chess
vukovic-art-of-attack.author: Vladimir Vukovic
vukovic-art-of-attack.note: The standard work on attacking the king. Source of the focal-point concept and of the precise conditions for the classic bishop sacrifice. ACCESS CAVEAT: read via the publisher's description and the Chessable summary, which quote Vukovic directly; the book itself has not been consulted.

gambit-art-of-attacking-chess.title: The Art of Attacking Chess (sample chapter: Opposite-Side Castling)
gambit-art-of-attacking-chess.author: Zenon Franco
gambit-art-of-attacking-chess.note: Publisher sample PDF read directly. Chapter 2 sets out the three scenarios in opposite-side castling: mutual race, attack against pure defence, and the modern combination of attack with prophylaxis on one's own wing.

chessable-art-of-attack.title: The Art of Attack in Chess: Updated Tactical Excellence
chessable-art-of-attack.author: Chessable
chessable-art-of-attack.note: Quotes Vukovic verbatim on focal-points and on the four conditions for the classic bishop sacrifice.

wikipedia-backward-pawn.title: Backward pawn
wikipedia-backward-pawn.author: Wikipedia contributors
wikipedia-backward-pawn.note: Definition: behind all pawns of the same colour on adjacent files, and cannot be safely advanced.

chessprogramming-rook-open-file.title: Rook on Open File
chessprogramming-rook-open-file.author: Chess Programming Wiki contributors
chessprogramming-rook-open-file.note: Gives a concrete engine-era number: bonuses for a rook on an open file range from about 8 to 20 centipawns. Also notes that Nimzowitsch used '(semi) open file' even for rooks standing in front of the pawn chain, which is a terminology difference from modern usage.

thechessworld-rooks-open-files.title: Total Chess: Rooks & Open Files
thechessworld-rooks-open-files.author: John Herron
thechessworld-rooks-open-files.note: Sets out the entry-point requirement: an open file is worth having only if there is a safe square deep in enemy territory to invade.

uscfsales-pawn-storm.title: When A Pawn Storm Can Make Sense
uscfsales-pawn-storm.note: Retailer blog. Used only for the uncontroversial observation that a pawn storm's aim is to open lines, corroborated by the Gambit and Modern Chess sources.

wikipedia-passed-pawn.title: Passed pawn
wikipedia-passed-pawn.author: Wikipedia contributors
wikipedia-passed-pawn.note: Definition, protected/connected/outside variants, and the Nimzowitsch 'criminal' quotation with a citation. Also the Botvinnik-Capablanca AVRO 1938 example of sacrificing to clear a passer's path.

chessprogramming-pawns-breakthrough.title: Pawns Breakthrough
chessprogramming-pawns-breakthrough.author: Chess Programming Wiki contributors
chessprogramming-pawns-breakthrough.note: Describes the canonical trio-versus-trio mechanism in engine terms (levers, rams).

pawnbreak-endgame-breaks.title: Pawn Breaks In The Endgame
pawnbreak-endgame-breaks.author: Simon Louchart
pawnbreak-endgame-breaks.note: Source of the space-advantage condition, stated testably: 'Move all pawns one row and the breakthrough does not work at all anymore.' That claim is engine-tested in the pawn-breakthrough record.

chessworld-pawn-breakthrough.title: Pawn Breakthrough Chess
chessworld-pawn-breakthrough.author: Tryfon Gavriel
chessworld-pawn-breakthrough.note: Three-step articulation: create two levers, sacrifice again to deflect, run the passer.

chesscom-passed-or-weak.title: Passed pawn or weak pawn?
chesscom-passed-or-weak.author: AjedrezdeSilicio
chesscom-passed-or-weak.note: Amateur blog, recorded for one well-put line that matches better sources: Nimzowitsch said every passed pawn must be blockaded 'and he was right - half the time'. Used as corroboration of the exception, not as authority.

naroditsky-rooks-seventh.title: Rooks on the Seventh, Revisited
naroditsky-rooks-seventh.author: GM Daniel Naroditsky
naroditsky-rooks-seventh.note: Grandmaster authorship, and unusually a CORRECTIVE piece: argues that two rooks on the seventh 'can almost never checkmate the king by themselves' when the eighth rank is defended, and that their power lies in mobility and restriction. Also attributes the nickname 'pigs on the seventh' to GM Yasser Seirawan's Winning Chess series.

oldschoolchess-rook-seventh.title: Rook on the 7th Rank
oldschoolchess-rook-seventh.note: Sets out Nimzowitsch's absolute-versus-relative seventh distinction clearly. Low confidence (anonymous); used for the distinction, which is corroborated by Naroditsky.

kingsights-good-bad-bishop.title: Good Bishop vs Bad Bishop
kingsights-good-bad-bishop.note: Anonymous. Recorded chiefly for one distinction it states well and which better sources support: Mihail Suba's 'active bad bishop' — a structurally bad bishop outside the pawn chain doing real work. 'Bad is structural; passive is functional.'

chessbio-doubled-pawns.title: Doubled pawns
chessbio-doubled-pawns.note: Anonymous. Notes the classical-versus-hypermodern disagreement over doubled pawns. Also carries the Capablanca line 'I would take doubled pawns if in return I may place my rook on the seventh rank' — explicitly prefaced 'Legend has it', and it is recorded as UNVERIFIED in the concept.

oldschoolchess-doubled-pawns.title: Doubled Pawns: Weakness or Weapon?
oldschoolchess-doubled-pawns.note: Good on the recapture decision and on compensations; anonymous, so used alongside the titled-player sources rather than alone.

thechessworld-doubled-pawns.title: Doubled Pawns: Weakness or Strength, Part 2
thechessworld-doubled-pawns.author: WGM Raluca Sgircea, IM Renier Castellanos
thechessworld-doubled-pawns.note: Titled authorship. Lists the three cases where doubled pawns are a strength: central control, creating outposts, and freeing one's own pieces via the opened file.

baburin-winning-pawn-structures.title: Winning Pawn Structures
baburin-winning-pawn-structures.author: GM Alexander Baburin
baburin-winning-pawn-structures.note: The standard work on the isolated queen's pawn. ACCESS CAVEAT: known here only through secondary discussion (Chess.com, Hacker News, pawnbreak.com); the book has not been read. Cited for its standing, not for wording.

pawnbreak-iqp.title: Introduction to the Isolated Queen's Pawn Positions
pawnbreak-iqp.author: Stjepan Tomic
pawnbreak-iqp.note: Frames the IQP as the thematic case of static weakness against dynamic compensation, which is the reason the structure is taught at all.

wikipedia-zugzwang.title: Zugzwang
wikipedia-zugzwang.author: Wikipedia contributors
wikipedia-zugzwang.note: Carries datable claims: the term appears in German chess literature in 1858 or earlier; the first known English use is Lasker, 1905; the CONCEPT appears in a 1604 Salvio study and in shatranj studies from the early 9th century. Also records the terminology split — some writers call the one-sided case a 'squeeze' and reserve 'zugzwang' for the reciprocal case.

winter-zugzwang.title: Zugzwang (Chess Notes)
winter-zugzwang.author: Edward Winter
winter-zugzwang.note: Winter on the term's origin: 'The first use of the word Zugzwang, ALLEGEDLY originated by Max Lange, needs to be determined.' That is an explicit statement that the attribution is unsettled, from the discipline's most careful historian, and it is why the zugzwang record carries confidence 'disputed' rather than naming Lange.

wikipedia-opposition.title: Opposition (chess)
wikipedia-opposition.author: Wikipedia contributors
wikipedia-opposition.note: Direct, diagonal and distant opposition; and Averbakh's corrective that the opposition is a means to an end, the end being penetration to a key square.

wikipedia-triangulation.title: Triangulation (chess)
wikipedia-triangulation.author: Wikipedia contributors
wikipedia-triangulation.note: Also called losing a tempo. Records that queen, rook and bishop can triangulate and a knight cannot.

wikipedia-corresponding-squares.title: Corresponding squares
wikipedia-corresponding-squares.author: Wikipedia contributors
wikipedia-corresponding-squares.note: 'The theory of corresponding squares is more general than opposition and is more useful in cluttered positions.' Records the Lasker-Reichhelm 1901 study and the 1932 Halberstadt and Duchamp treatise.

lichess-tablebase.title: Lichess tablebase (Syzygy, 7-piece)
lichess-tablebase.author: Lichess
lichess-tablebase.note: Proof, not evaluation, for positions of seven pieces or fewer. Queried by education/tools/tablebase.py. Where a result comes from here it outranks any engine evaluation and the concept is typed tablebase-fact.

chessworld-initiative.title: Chess Initiative Adviser: Tempo & Morphy Games
chessworld-initiative.author: Tryfon Gavriel
chessworld-initiative.note: Clear on the tempo/initiative distinction and on the two-jobs test for a gained tempo.

playchessonline-tempo-initiative.title: Chess Tempo & Initiative
playchessonline-tempo-initiative.note: Anonymous. Recorded for one honest statement worth keeping: 'A tempo has no universal pawn value' — which is the right corrective to the widespread habit of pricing a tempo at a third of a pawn.

lichess-steinitz-advantages.title: Steinitz's Advantages (study)
lichess-steinitz-advantages.note: A community study enumerating Steinitz's list of advantages, split into permanent and temporary. Low confidence as a source for what Steinitz actually wrote; used only as a pointer to the permanent/temporary division, which is corroborated elsewhere.

chessprogramming-king-safety.title: King Safety
chessprogramming-king-safety.author: Chess Programming Wiki contributors
chessprogramming-king-safety.note: Unusually valuable because it states how Stockfish actually evaluates king safety, with numbers: the king zone is the squares the enemy king can reach plus three forward squares; a minor-piece attack on it counts 2 attack units, a rook 3, a queen 5, with 6 more for a safe queen contact check; the resulting attack score is looked up in an S-shaped table. It also records the practical rule that king attack is not worth evaluating with fewer than three attackers.

chessworld-king-safety.title: Chess King Safety Adviser
chessworld-king-safety.author: Tryfon Gavriel
chessworld-king-safety.note: Good on hooks and on the point that castling and king safety are not the same thing.

chesswoodie-opening-principles.title: Chess Opening Principles: The 5 Rules and When to Break Them
chesswoodie-opening-principles.note: Anonymous, but framed around the exceptions rather than the rules, which is the part this project needs. Corroborated on each specific exception by other sources.

chessstrategyonline-opening.title: How to Start a Game of Chess: Opening Principles
chessstrategyonline-opening.note: The conventional five-rule list, with the capture exception to the same-piece-twice rule stated explicitly.

wikipedia-lucena.title: Lucena position
wikipedia-lucena.author: Wikipedia contributors
wikipedia-lucena.note: Carries the documented MISATTRIBUTION with its trail: the position does not appear in Lucena's 1497 book; the earliest preserved discussion is Salvio's Il Puttino (1634), who attributes it to Scipione Genovino; and the error is traced to Constantin Schwede's sixth edition of the Handbuch des Schachspiels (1880). Also quotes Karsten Müller calling it possibly the most important position in endgame theory.

wikipedia-philidor-position.title: Philidor position
wikipedia-philidor-position.author: Wikipedia contributors
wikipedia-philidor-position.note: Analysed by Philidor in 1777. Records that Karstedt (1897) and Berger showed Philidor's belief that the third-rank defence was the ONLY drawing method is not strictly true, though the alternatives are more complicated.

chessbase-vancura.title: Karsten Müller: Understanding the Vancura draw
chessbase-vancura.author: GM Karsten Müller
chessbase-vancura.note: Written by the endgame authority who edited Dvoretsky's Endgame Manual. Gives the position with full analysis, the g7/h7 drawing zone and the reason for it (otherwise Rh8 and Rh7+ skewers), and the Carlsen-Aronian 2014 game where the defence held.

naroditsky-two-rook-endings.title: The Two Rook Endings You Must Know
naroditsky-two-rook-endings.author: GM Daniel Naroditsky
naroditsky-two-rook-endings.note: Grandmaster treatment of Philidor and Lucena, including why the two defensive tries against Philidor both fail.

chessbio-building-a-bridge.title: Building a bridge
chessbio-building-a-bridge.note: Anonymous. Used for the 'umbrella technique' synonym and the step list, both corroborated elsewhere.

chessmind-vancura.title: Vancura Position: Drawing vs the Rook Pawn
chessmind-vancura.author: ChessMind AI
chessmind-vancura.note: AI-authored. Recorded for one formulation that the tablebase then confirmed exactly: 'behind the pawn, the rook attacks a square the pawn will leave; beside the pawn, it attacks the square the pawn lives on'. Also gives Vancura's dates (1898-1921) and the 1924 posthumous publication, which match ChessBase.

wikipedia-wrong-rook-pawn.title: Wrong rook pawn
wikipedia-wrong-rook-pawn.author: Wikipedia contributors
wikipedia-wrong-rook-pawn.note: Dates the knowledge to at least 1623 via a Gioachino Greco study. Cites Müller & Lamprecht, Mednis, Fine & Benko and de la Villa for the specific cases. Also records the Kasparov-Ķeņģis game where the ten-year-old Kasparov thought he was winning two pawns up and it was drawn.

wikipedia-wrong-bishop.title: Wrong bishop
wikipedia-wrong-bishop.author: Wikipedia contributors
wikipedia-wrong-bishop.note: Covers the mirror cases: rook versus bishop, rook and rook pawn versus bishop, and the 'safe corner' idea. Notes del Rio studied the bishop-pawn case around 1750.

chessprogramming-wrong-bishop.title: Wrong Color Bishop and Rook Pawn
chessprogramming-wrong-bishop.author: Chess Programming Wiki contributors
chessprogramming-wrong-bishop.note: States the engine-era fact plainly: this is a drawn fortress that 'needs to be encoded in the evaluation function, as search would not evaluate them properly'. Cites TCEC Season 5 Superfinal, where Komodo had the knowledge and Stockfish apparently did not.

wikipedia-ocb.title: Opposite-colored bishops endgame
wikipedia-ocb.author: Wikipedia contributors
wikipedia-ocb.note: Gives the concrete statistics: about half of bishop-and-four-pawns versus opposite-coloured-bishop endings are drawn, against over 90% wins when the bishops are on the same colour. Also the separated-pawns rule and the deliberate bad-bishop defensive idea.

lichess-dvoretsky-fortress.title: Fortresses in Pawn Endgames (study)
lichess-dvoretsky-fortress.note: Carries Dvoretsky's definition — a situation in which a king, with or without the assistance of pieces or pawns, successfully defends a small territory. ACCESS CAVEAT: quoted via a community study, not from Dvoretsky's text.

chessify-engine-eval.title: Behind the Numbers: Understanding Chess Engine Evaluations
chessify-engine-eval.note: Used only for the uncontroversial statement that engines misevaluate fortresses and that tablebase integration is the standard remedy; corroborated by the Chess Programming Wiki.

wikipedia-hypermodernism.title: Hypermodernism (chess)
wikipedia-hypermodernism.author: Wikipedia contributors
wikipedia-hypermodernism.note: Names Tartakower as the originator of the term 'hypermodern' (his Die hypermoderne Schachpartie, 1924), Réti's Die neuen Ideen im Schachspiel (1922) and Nimzowitsch's Mein System (1925-27). Also the key conclusion: hypermodernism did not replace classical theory, and textbooks treat it as an extension of it.

britannica-chess-theory-3.title: The Evolution of Chess Theory, Part 3
britannica-chess-theory-3.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
britannica-chess-theory-3.note: Traces the sequence Romantic -> Classical -> Hypermodern -> Soviet. Carries Breyer's joke and Réti's line that the new generation was interested not in rules but in exceptions, and describes the Soviet school's elevation of the initiative and its willingness to accept structures earlier schools called bad.

wikibooks-chess-centre.title: Chess Strategy: The center
wikibooks-chess-centre.author: Wikibooks contributors
wikibooks-chess-centre.note: Community-written. Used for the 'Russian dynamism' framing and the rule that a wing attack depends on control of the centre, both corroborated by Britannica.

scribd-hypermodern-revolt.title: The Center is a Target: The Hypermodern Revolt
scribd-hypermodern-revolt.note: Anonymous uploaded document. Recorded for two things: the five-centre typology, and one unusually honest formulation — 'Hypermodern play is correct as a correction and false as a dogma'. CAUTION: it attributes 'rooks belong behind passed pawns' to TARTAKOWER, where other sources say Tarrasch. That disagreement is now recorded on the passed-pawn concept rather than silently resolved.

kaufman-material-imbalances.title: The Evaluation of Material Imbalances
kaufman-material-imbalances.author: IM Larry Kaufman
kaufman-material-imbalances.note: Statistical study over a large game sample by a titled player who later worked on Komodo. Source of the piece values used in modern engines: knight 3.5, unpaired bishop 3.5, rook 5.25, bishop PAIR 7.5, queen 10 — so the pair is worth about half a pawn beyond the two bishops. Also the exchange at 1.75 pawns and the 'redundancy of major pieces' principle.

heisman-kaufman-values.title: Evaluation of Material Imbalances (annotated)
heisman-kaufman-values.author: Dan Heisman
heisman-kaufman-values.note: Carries Kaufman's figures with a coach's annotations, including the observation that the fewer pieces on the board, the fewer pawns a minor piece is worth.

chessdigits-imbalances.title: Material Imbalances and Game Outcomes
chessdigits-imbalances.note: Empirical outcome study over a large game database. Its headline finding contradicts received wisdom: with queen against two rooks the QUEEN wins 49% and the rooks 31%. It also confirms two minor pieces over a rook (rook loses 66% to two bishops) and the bishop pair. Anonymous, so recorded medium and used alongside Kaufman rather than alone.

silman-reassess.title: How to Reassess Your Chess (4th ed.)
silman-reassess.author: IM Jeremy Silman
silman-reassess.note: Full text consulted. Source of the imbalance framework: 'an imbalance is any significant difference in the two respective positions', with the list — superior minor piece, pawn structure, space, material, files and squares, development, initiative — used as the roadmap for choosing a plan.

studer-bishop-vs-knight.title: Bishop vs Knight In Chess: A Grandmaster Guide
studer-bishop-vs-knight.author: GM Noël Studer
studer-bishop-vs-knight.note: Grandmaster authorship, and unusually sceptical: he notes that the common claim that a bishop is worth 3.5 against a knight's 3 or 3.25 'is not funded with evidence' and that he knows of no statistic supporting it. Also the advanced colour rule — with two knights and a bishop, play on your bishop's colour; with two bishops and a knight, play on the colour of the bishop your opponent lacks.

chessstack-bishop-knight.title: Bishop vs Knight (Chess Stack Exchange)
chessstack-bishop-knight.note: Forum thread; low confidence by default. Recorded for two things corroborated elsewhere: the Kasparov remark that bishops are better in general because more positions favour them, and the observation that a knight PAIR is redundant because knights compete for the same outpost while bishops complement each other.

thechessworld-bishop-better.title: When a Bishop is Better Than a Knight
thechessworld-bishop-better.author: WGM Raluca Sgircea, IM Renier Castellanos
thechessworld-bishop-better.note: Titled authorship. Gives the four conditions favouring the bishop, including that rook and bishop usually beat rook and knight.

chessstrategyonline-exchanges.title: Introduction to Chess Strategy: Exchanges
chessstrategyonline-exchanges.note: Anonymous. Used for the conventional exchanging rules, which are uncontroversial and corroborated widely.

wikipedia-chess-opening.title: Chess opening
wikipedia-chess-opening.author: Wikipedia contributors
wikipedia-chess-opening.note: Used for the objectives of the opening, the repertoire notion, the naming terminology and the definition of a theoretical novelty / prepared variation.

wikipedia-gambit.title: Gambit
wikipedia-gambit.author: Wikipedia contributors
wikipedia-gambit.note: Etymology (Ruy Lopez 1561, Beale 1656), the three soundness criteria, and the explicit hedge that the three-tempi maxim's usefulness 'is unclear'.

murray-history-of-chess.title: A History of Chess
murray-history-of-chess.author: H.J.R. Murray
murray-history-of-chess.note: Page 813, for Ruy Lopez's own derivation of 'gambit' from gamba/gambitare (Lopez fol. 108a). Consulted at second hand via Winter, not read directly - flagged because this base treats quotation chains as a known failure mode.

winter-chess-gambits.title: Chess Gambits (Chess Notes feature article)
winter-chess-gambits.author: Edward Winter
winter-chess-gambits.note: The primary check on the Steinitz 'refute a gambit by accepting it' attribution. Winter documents the wording drifting between 'gambit' and 'sacrifice' across sources and treats it as unverified.

exeter-gambits.title: Gambits
exeter-gambits.author: Exeter Chess Club (Dr Dave Regis)
exeter-gambits.note: Source of the tempo-counting refinement (count moves still needed, not moves made) and of the defensive recipe of returning material to complete development.

chessmind-gambit.title: Gambit in Chess: Sacrificing Pawns for the Initiative
chessmind-gambit.author: ChessMind AI
chessmind-gambit.note: AI-authored site. Used only for framing that this base verified independently; not relied on for any factual claim on its own.

chessmind-transposition.title: Transposition in Chess: Move Orders Explained
chessmind-transposition.author: ChessMind AI
chessmind-transposition.note: AI-authored site. The statement of what a position does and does not remember was checked against the FIDE Laws before use.

chessstack-tabiya.title: What is a tabiya and what is their importance?
chessstack-tabiya.author: Chess Stack Exchange
chessstack-tabiya.note: Community answers. The shatranj etymology given there is recorded as uncertain rather than asserted; one answer claims Sanskrit origin and another Arabic, and they are not reconciled.

wiktionary-tabiya.title: tabiya
wiktionary-tabiya.author: Wiktionary
wiktionary-tabiya.note: Definition plus attested usages from published opening books.

morphy-move-by-move.title: Morphy: Move by Move (extract)
morphy-move-by-move.author: Zenon Franco
morphy-move-by-move.note: Extract consulted directly. Carries Euwe's three-element summary of Morphy's style and Kasparov's annotations quoted within.

chessstrategyonline-opening-principles.title: Opening principles
chessstrategyonline-opening-principles.author: Chess Strategy Online
chessstrategyonline-opening-principles.note: A standard statement of the beginner principle list, used for the canonical wording of the rules.

chessify-novelties.title: 7 Exclusive Grandmaster Tips on How to Find Chess Opening Novelties
chessify-novelties.author: Chessify
chessify-novelties.note: Commercial engine-hosting blog. Used only for the uncontroversial observation that elite novelties are engine-generated and engine-checked.

teamliquid-computers-changed-chess.title: A brief history of how computers changed chess forever
teamliquid-computers-changed-chess.author: TeamLiquid
teamliquid-computers-changed-chess.note: Popular history. Used for the claim that engine preparation has made narrow opening specialisation harder at elite level; corroborated in outline by the Wikipedia opening article, but treated as low confidence.

binet-1894.title: Psychologie des grands calculateurs et joueurs d'echecs
binet-1894.author: Alfred Binet
binet-1894.note: The first scientific study of chess memory, based on questionnaires sent to leading blindfold players. Consulted through Gobet's and Campitelli & Gobet's summaries, NOT read in the original French - flagged because this base treats quotation chains as a known failure mode. An English abridgement appeared as 'Mnemonic virtuosity: a study of chess players' (1966).

fine-1965-blindfold.title: The psychology of blindfold chess: an introspective account
fine-1965-blindfold.author: Reuben Fine
fine-1965-blindfold.note: Acta Psychologica 24(4):352-370. A world-class player's own introspective account. Consulted through Campitelli & Gobet's summary, not read directly.

chase-simon-1973.title: Perception in chess
chase-simon-1973.author: William G. Chase and Herbert A. Simon
chase-simon-1973.note: Full text consulted directly. Source of the chunking account and of the five measured chunk relations (attack, defence, proximity, common colour, common type).

campitelli-gobet-2004.title: The mind's eye in blindfold chess
campitelli-gobet-2004.author: Guillermo Campitelli and Fernand Gobet
campitelli-gobet-2004.note: Full text consulted directly. The central review of the blindfold-chess literature and the source for most of the experimental findings recorded here.

gobet-memory-chunks-schemata.title: Memory in chess players: chunks, schemata, or both?
gobet-memory-chunks-schemata.author: Fernand Gobet
gobet-memory-chunks-schemata.note: Full text consulted directly. Detailed account of Binet, de Groot and Chase & Simon, including Binet's reversal of his own hypothesis.

saariluoma-kalakoski-1998.title: Apperception and Imagery in Blindfold Chess
saariluoma-kalakoski-1998.author: Pertti Saariluoma and Virpi Kalakoski
saariluoma-kalakoski-1998.note: Memory 6(1):67-90. Abstract read directly; the functional-figure finding is stated there. The detailed experiments are known through Campitelli & Gobet.

chesscom-blindfold-exercises.title: 7 Levels of Blindfold Chess Exercises for Everyone
chesscom-blindfold-exercises.author: Chess.com (AdviceCabinet)
chesscom-blindfold-exercises.note: Popular training article. Used only for the standard drill progression, which is corroborated across several instructional sources.

darksquares-blindfold-drills.title: 10 Classic Drills Masters Use to Train Blindfold Visualization
darksquares-blindfold-drills.author: Dark Squares
darksquares-blindfold-drills.note: Instructional blog. Source of the Najdorf and Koltanowski record claims, which are NOT independently verified here.

chessworld-visualisation.title: Chess Visualization Training - Adviser & Practice / Blindfold Practice Lab
chessworld-visualisation.author: ChessWorld.net
chessworld-visualisation.note: Interactive training site. Used only for the drill progression, which is corroborated across several instructional sources. Makes transfer-to-strength claims that this base does not repeat.

kotov-think-like-gm.title: Think Like a Grandmaster
kotov-think-like-gm.author: Alexander Kotov
kotov-think-like-gm.note: The origin of the candidate-moves technique and the tree of analysis. Written in the early 1950s; the widely cited English edition is 1971. Known here through detailed secondary accounts (Leitao, van Delft, Nunn's critique), not read directly.

dvoretsky-attack-and-defence.title: Attack and Defence
dvoretsky-attack-and-defence.author: Mark Dvoretsky and Artur Yusupov
dvoretsky-attack-and-defence.note: Chapter 1 on the technique of analysis and decision-taking, plus Krasenkow's guest chapter 'Wandering in the jungle'. Known through the Chessable research paper's summary, not read directly.

tisdall-improve-your-chess-now.title: Improve Your Chess Now
tisdall-improve-your-chess-now.author: Jonathan Tisdall
tisdall-improve-your-chess-now.note: Source of the single-critical-variation approach and the argument that candidate lists are not the primary task. Known through a detailed reader's notes page, not read directly.

leitao-candidate-moves.title: The Candidate Moves Technique
leitao-candidate-moves.author: Rafael Leitao
leitao-candidate-moves.note: Read directly. A grandmaster's assessment, including the concrete demonstration that Kotov's own worked analysis misses candidate moves and contains a miscalculation.

chessable-candidate-moves-research.title: Candidate moves (research paper)
chessable-candidate-moves-research.author: Karel van Delft and the Chessable science team
chessable-candidate-moves-research.note: Read directly. Surveys Kotov, Nunn, Dvoretsky, Krasenkow, Leitao and others, and includes an interview with Yusupov. Commercially motivated (it advertises a course), so used for its survey of positions rather than its conclusions.

chessmind-candidate-moves.title: Candidate Moves in Chess: Kotov's Method
chessmind-candidate-moves.author: ChessMind AI
chessmind-candidate-moves.note: AI-authored site. Used only where it agrees with the named grandmaster sources.

chessentials-endgame-strategy-review.title: Endgame Strategy - Book review
chessentials-endgame-strategy-review.author: Bruno Pavcevic (Chessentials)
chessentials-endgame-strategy-review.note: Used for the book's chapter structure and its three-part working definition of when an endgame has arisen.

oldschoolchess-capablanca-endgame.title: Capablanca vs Tartakower 1924: Endgame Mastery
oldschoolchess-capablanca-endgame.author: OldSchoolChess
oldschoolchess-capablanca-endgame.note: Instructional game annotation. Used only for uncontroversial framing of rook activity; no factual claim rests on it alone.

serper-positional-secret.title: The Biggest Secret Of Positional Chess
serper-positional-secret.author: GM Gregory Serper (Chess.com)
serper-positional-secret.note: A grandmaster's survey of the worst-piece rule and, valuably, of its four competing names. Source of the Anderssen, Makogonov/Mikhalchishin, Botvinnik-on-Fischer and Dvoretsky formulations, each quoted there.

hooper-steinitz-theory.title: Steinitz' Theory, British Chess Magazine Vol. 104, p.370
hooper-steinitz-theory.author: David Hooper
hooper-steinitz-theory.note: The seven numbered propositions of Steinitz's accumulation theory. Quoted at second hand via the Exeter Chess Club page, not read directly.

exeter-steinitz-accumulation.title: When and where to attack (Steinitz' accumulation theory)
exeter-steinitz-accumulation.author: Exeter Chess Club (Dr Dave Regis)
exeter-steinitz-accumulation.note: Carries Hooper's seven propositions verbatim, Steinitz's element lists, and Lasker's maxim on combinations.

chesswise-strategic-elements.title: Strategic Elements
chesswise-strategic-elements.author: ChessWise
chesswise-strategic-elements.note: A second, independently presented copy of the permanent/temporary advantage lists, used to corroborate the Exeter version. Notes explicitly that the lists are a REFINED version rather than Steinitz's own words.

thechessworld-planning.title: How to Create a Plan in Chess (Even When You Feel Lost)
thechessworld-planning.author: Prasanna Kumar (TheChessWorld)
thechessworld-planning.note: Four-step planning framework and, more useful here, a clear statement of the common planning errors.

chessmood-7q-planning.title: The 7Q Method: How to Make a Plan in Any Chess Position
chessmood-7q-planning.author: ChessMood
chessmood-7q-planning.note: A commercial training method. Used only as a second example of question-driven planning frameworks, not for any factual claim.

turzo-worst-piece-critique.title: Why 'Improve Your Worst Piece' Is Often Not Enough
turzo-worst-piece-critique.author: Attila Turzo
turzo-worst-piece-critique.note: Blog post advertising a course, so treated with care; used only for the criticism that principles do not establish priority, which is independently supported by the preconditions built into Anderssen's and Makogonov's own formulations.

polugaevsky-art-of-defence.title: The Art of Defence in Chess
polugaevsky-art-of-defence.author: Lev Polugaevsky (with Iakov Damsky)
polugaevsky-art-of-defence.note: Text consulted directly. Source of the three-way division of defence (passive, active, combinational), the defensive-procedure analysis of Kasparov-Andersson 1981, and the defence-by-simplification-into-drawish-endings method.

exeter-theory-of-steinitz.title: The Theory of Steinitz
exeter-theory-of-steinitz.author: Exeter Chess Club (Dr Dave Regis)
exeter-theory-of-steinitz.note: Carries Hooper's seven propositions and, importantly, the claim that proposition 4 was first indicated by Louis Paulsen, making him the progenitor of Steinitz's theory. Also the minimum-concession rule and the Purdy quotation.

markushin-defensive-principles.title: How to Defend in Chess - 7 Most Important Defense Principles
markushin-defensive-principles.author: Yury Markushin (TheChessWorld)
markushin-defensive-principles.note: A standard club-level statement of defensive principles. Notably advises simplifying when short of space, which conflicts with the practical advice to complicate when worse; the conflict is recorded on the concept rather than smoothed over.

turzo-saving-bad-positions.title: How to Save a Bad Chess Position: 6 Defensive Strategies
turzo-saving-bad-positions.author: Attila Turzo
turzo-saving-bad-positions.note: Blog post advertising a course. Used only for the practical-chances view of defence, which is corroborated by Polugaevsky's treatment; no factual claim rests on it alone.

chessbase-nimzowitsch-precepts.title: The Nimzowitsch precepts of positional chess
chessbase-nimzowitsch-precepts.author: ChessBase (Dennis Monokroussos)
chessbase-nimzowitsch-precepts.note: Source of Reuben Fine's summary of Nimzowitsch's method as 'restrict, blockade, destroy'.

dvoretsky-yusupov-technique.title: Technique in Chess
dvoretsky-yusupov-technique.author: Mark Dvoretsky and Artur Yusupov
dvoretsky-yusupov-technique.note: Text consulted directly. Source of the Four Golden Principles of Technique and of the transformation-of-an-advantage and concrete-play sections, including the authors' own statement that concrete play runs contrary to the golden principles.

kane-technique-review.title: Technique in Chess (review)
kane-technique-review.author: Paul Kane
kane-technique-review.note: Records a substantive disagreement with the authors over whether concrete play is contrary to the golden principles, and supplies the Zaitsev and Gligoric definitions of technique.

chessbase-karpov-coordination.title: The Winning Academy 10: Karpov's Secret Weapon
chessbase-karpov-coordination.author: ChessBase (Jan Markos)
chessbase-karpov-coordination.note: On manoeuvring and coordination as the skill for positions where neither side has an active plan.

collins-karpov-move-by-move.title: Karpov: Move by Move
collins-karpov-move-by-move.author: Sam Collins
collins-karpov-move-by-move.note: Consulted directly. Carries Karpov's and Dvoretsky's own comments on coordination and prophylaxis, quoted within.

dvoretsky-maneuvering.title: Maneuvering: the Art of Piece Play
dvoretsky-maneuvering.author: Mark Dvoretsky
dvoretsky-maneuvering.note: Known only from its publisher description; not read. Cited for the existence of a dedicated treatment of piece improvement when no forcing line or obvious plan exists.

fide-laws-appendix-c.title: FIDE Laws of Chess, Appendix C: Algebraic Notation
fide-laws-appendix-c.author: FIDE
fide-laws-appendix-c.note: The only notation FIDE recognises for official play. Consulted alongside the main Laws text already held in research/fide-laws-2023.md.

wikipedia-chess-notation.title: Chess notation / Algebraic notation / Descriptive notation
wikipedia-chess-notation.author: Wikipedia contributors
wikipedia-chess-notation.note: Used for the historical descriptive system and the relationship between the notations; the normative claims are taken from the FIDE Laws instead.

wikipedia-rule-of-the-square.title: Rule of the square
wikipedia-rule-of-the-square.author: Wikipedia contributors
wikipedia-rule-of-the-square.note: Standard statement of the rule. The claim itself is verified in this base against the Syzygy tablebase rather than taken on the source's authority.

wikipedia-chess-piece-values.title: Chess piece relative value
wikipedia-chess-piece-values.author: Wikipedia contributors
wikipedia-chess-piece-values.note: Survey of the competing value systems. This base records the disagreement rather than adopting one; see the knight-vs-bishop record for the sharpest instance.

botvinnik-what-is-a-combination.title: What is a 'combination'? (appendix to One Hundred Selected Games)
botvinnik-what-is-a-combination.author: Mikhail Botvinnik
botvinnik-what-is-a-combination.note: The definition that started the argument, first published in Chess in the USSR (1939). Known here through two independent secondary accounts that quote it directly, not read in the original.

romanovsky-mittelshpiel.title: Mittelshpiel
romanovsky-mittelshpiel.author: Peter Romanovsky
romanovsky-mittelshpiel.note: The competing definition, which does not require a sacrifice. Quoted at second hand; it was the basis for the Chess Dictionary's 1964 entry.

chesswatch-what-is-a-combination.title: What is a combination? (Karlson, part 1)
chesswatch-what-is-a-combination.author: Serhii Serdiuk (ChessWatch)
chesswatch-what-is-a-combination.note: A detailed history of the Soviet debate over the definition, naming the participants, dates and journals, including Averbakh's 1980 reversal. English translation of a Ukrainian-language article; the quotations are consistent with the Mark Weeks page consulted independently.

weeks-combinations.title: Improve Your Middle Game (Part 2 - Combinations)
weeks-combinations.author: Mark Weeks
weeks-combinations.note: Independent second source for the Lasker, Botvinnik and Hooper & Whyld definitions, including Botvinnik's own two endgame examples distinguishing a combination from a manoeuvre.

hooper-whyld-oxford-companion.title: The Oxford Companion to Chess
hooper-whyld-oxford-companion.author: David Hooper and Kenneth Whyld
hooper-whyld-oxford-companion.note: Quoted at second hand for the combination entry, which explicitly reports the disagreement rather than settling it.

wikipedia-chess-endgame.title: Chess endgame
wikipedia-chess-endgame.author: Wikipedia contributors
wikipedia-chess-endgame.note: Used for the survey of endgame types by material, the Botvinnik quotation on knight endings, and the note that queen-and-pawn endings resisted complete human analysis until tablebases.

chessphd-queen-endgame.title: Queen endgame in Chess - Explained
chessphd-queen-endgame.author: Chess.PhD
chessphd-queen-endgame.note: Short instructional page. Used only for the practical framing (shelter the king, centralise the queen, bail out into perpetual check), which is corroborated by Dvoretsky's worked examples.

sigman-response-times-2010.title: Response time distributions in rapid chess: a large-scale decision making experiment
sigman-response-times-2010.author: Mariano Sigman, Pablo Etchemendy, Diego Fernandez Slezak, Guillermo A. Cecchi
sigman-response-times-2010.note: Frontiers in Neuroscience 4:60. Over 91,000 games. Source of the time-allocation profile by game phase and of the finding that an 8-second edge equals an extra knight under severe time pressure. Known through de Lafuente's detailed review, not read in the original.

delafuente-flexible-decisions.title: Flexible Decisions and Chess Expertise
delafuente-flexible-decisions.author: Victor de Lafuente
delafuente-flexible-decisions.note: Read directly. A detailed review of Sigman et al. (2010), including the board-entropy analysis and the shift from material to time as the determinant of outcome.

harreveld-time-pressure.title: The effects of time pressure on chess skill: an investigation into fast and slow processes underlying expert performance
harreveld-time-pressure.author: Frenk van Harreveld, Eric-Jan Wagenmakers, Han L. J. van der Maas
harreveld-time-pressure.note: Full text consulted directly. Source of the finding that normal-time rating becomes less predictive once players are forced to play fast, and of the survey of de Groot, Charness and Holding on search depth versus width.

vidulich-tsang-intuition.title: Intuition and deliberation in elite expertise
vidulich-tsang-intuition.author: Michael A. Vidulich and Pamela S. Tsang
vidulich-tsang-intuition.note: Abstract read directly. Twenty grandmasters and seven world champions; finds strong adverse time-pressure effects and concludes that deliberation remains essential even at the highest level, against the view that expertise is primarily intuitive.

carow-witzig-risk.title: Time pressure and strategic risk-taking in professional chess
carow-witzig-risk.author: Johannes Carow and Niklas M. Witzig
carow-witzig-risk.note: Abstract read directly. FIDE World Cups 2013-2023: less thinking time leads to more risk-averse moves, most strongly in bad positions, with correlational evidence for more risk-taking after a mistake.

blitz-error-amplification-2026.title: Interpretable machine learning analysis of nonlinear error amplification under time pressure and positional ambiguity in elite blitz chess
blitz-error-amplification-2026.author: Scientific Reports
blitz-error-amplification-2026.note: Abstract read directly. Nearly 40,000 blitz positions; blunder probability amplifies nonlinearly under combined time pressure and positional ambiguity rather than adding independently.

watson-secrets-modern-strategy.title: Secrets of Modern Chess Strategy
watson-secrets-modern-strategy.author: John Watson
watson-secrets-modern-strategy.note: Cited at second hand for the thesis that modern high-level play rests on concrete analysis rather than rule-based thinking, and that this is the core of the modern Soviet school. Not read directly.

capablanca-tartakower-1924.title: Capablanca - Tartakower, New York 1924 (game score and annotations)
capablanca-tartakower-1924.author: chessgames.com; annotations by Alekhine and Chernev via A.J. Goldsby
capablanca-tartakower-1924.note: The move list was taken from two independent sources that agree, and then REPLAYED through the page's own move generator by tools/replay_game.js — all 103 plies legal — so every FEN derived from it is verified rather than transcribed. Alekhine's and Chernev's annotations are quoted at second hand from a page reproducing them.

nimzowitsch-salwe-1911.title: Nimzowitsch - Salwe, Karlsbad 1911 (game score with Nimzowitsch's own notes)
nimzowitsch-salwe-1911.author: Aron Nimzowitsch
nimzowitsch-salwe-1911.note: The canonical illustration of the blockade, annotated by the player who formulated the concept. All 77 plies replayed successfully through the page's own move generator, so the derived FENs are verified.

umbc-carlsbad-lesson.title: Lesson 12: Strategic Ideas in the Carlsbad Pawn Structure
umbc-carlsbad-lesson.author: Alan T. Sherman (UMBC master-prep lectures)
umbc-carlsbad-lesson.note: Source of Nimzowitsch's formulation that the numerical minority is a QUALITATIVE majority, and of the Petrosian-Krogius game score. NOTE: the score as printed there fails to replay at Black's 24th move (Ra3 is not legal); the first 46 plies verify and are what this base uses.

thechessworld-minority-attack.title: The Queen's Gambit: The Minority Attack in the Carlsbad Pawn Structure
thechessworld-minority-attack.author: WGM Raluca Sgircea and IM Renier Castellanos
thechessworld-minority-attack.note: Source of the mechanism (Rb1, b4-b5 without moving the a-pawn, bxc6) and the resulting targets on a7 and c6.

thechessworld-carlsbad-karpov.title: The Carlsbad Structure - Anatoly Karpov's Way
thechessworld-carlsbad-karpov.author: WGM Raluca Sgircea and IM Renier Castellanos
thechessworld-carlsbad-karpov.note: Source of the caution that the attack must not be forced through mechanically, and of Karpov's alternative manoeuvres around c5.

petrosian-krogius-1959.title: Petrosian - Krogius, Tbilisi 1959 (game score)
petrosian-krogius-1959.author: via UMBC master-prep lecture notes
petrosian-krogius-1959.note: First 46 plies replayed successfully through the page's own move generator, so the FENs derived from them are verified. The source's move 24 for Black does not replay and the remainder is therefore NOT used or cited here.

zurich-1953-games.title: Candidates Tournament, Zurich 1953 — game scores
zurich-1953-games.author: ChessBase shared game collection
zurich-1953-games.note: Full PGN with headers. Four games were taken from it — Smyslov-Petrosian, Petrosian-Euwe, Kotov-Petrosian and Stahlberg-Petrosian — and ALL FOUR replay legally end to end through the page's own move generator (95, 123, 66 and 128 plies), so every FEN derived from them is verified rather than transcribed. That check has already rejected a score from a different source, so passing it is meaningful.

naroditsky-petrosian-exchange-sacs.title: Tigran Petrosian's Breathtaking Exchange Sacrifices
naroditsky-petrosian-exchange-sacs.author: GM Daniel Naroditsky (Chess.com)
naroditsky-petrosian-exchange-sacs.note: Source of the three-way classification of exchange sacrifices — prophylactic, positional, tactical — with Reshevsky-Petrosian 1953 given as the PROPHYLACTIC example. Also carries Kasparov's judgement that Petrosian sacrificed 'for the sake of quality of position'.

chessgames-reshevsky-petrosian-1953.title: Reshevsky - Petrosian, Zurich Candidates 1953 (game and annotations)
chessgames-reshevsky-petrosian-1953.author: chessgames.com, with Watson's and Kasparov's comments quoted there
chessgames-reshevsky-petrosian-1953.note: Carries Petrosian's own reasoning as reported by Watson — he disliked his position, foresaw h4 provoking kingside weakness, and searched for a way to reach d5 with a knight. All 81 plies replay legally through the page's own move generator.

amazingatlas-rubinstein-salwe.title: Game 20: Rubinstein vs Salwe, Lodz 1908 - How to Squeeze a Weak Pawn
amazingatlas-rubinstein-salwe.author: Nicholas Van Der Nat (Chess.com)
amazingatlas-rubinstein-salwe.note: Modern annotation of a game that is a fixture of the classical literature. Used for the explicit concept attributions - two weaknesses, the bad bishop on e6, restriction - not for novel claims. The game score replays legally end to end through the page's own move generator.

thechessworld-hanging-pawns.title: Fundamental Pawn Structures: Hanging Pawns
thechessworld-hanging-pawns.author: WGM Raluca Sgircea and IM Renier Castellanos
thechessworld-hanging-pawns.note: Source of the definition, the standard method against them (force one to advance and blockade the square it leaves), and the openings they arise from.

lichess-fischer-spassky-g6.title: Fischer - Spassky, Reykjavik 1972, game 6 (annotated study)
lichess-fischer-spassky-g6.author: lichess study by flohahn22, following the standard literature
lichess-fischer-spassky-g6.note: Move-by-move annotations that NAME the concepts: 'we've reached a position with hanging pawns' at move 16, the restriction of the h7 knight at move 30, and the fixing of Black's pawns on light squares to favour the bishop at move 22. All 81 plies replay legally through the page's own move generator. Corroborated on the moves by chessgames.com and on the assessment by a Chess.com retrospective.

chesscom-fischer-spassky-g6.title: Bobby Fischer Wins Positional Masterpiece (50-year retrospective)
chesscom-fischer-spassky-g6.author: Anthony Levin (Chess.com)
chesscom-fischer-spassky-g6.note: Independent corroboration that 13.Qa3 pressured 'what would become hanging pawns on c5 and d5', and that 20...d4? was the positional error that left a weak pawn on e6.

dgriffin-botvinnik-smyslov-1954-g1.title: Smyslov-Botvinnik, 1st match-game, World Championship, Moscow 1954 - annotations by M. Botvinnik
dgriffin-botvinnik-smyslov-1954-g1.author: Mikhail Botvinnik; translated from the Russian by Douglas Griffin
dgriffin-botvinnik-smyslov-1954-g1.note: Botvinnik's own notes to his own game, from his book of the 1954 match (Fizkultura i Sport, 1955), in Douglas Griffin's translation. Used for one thing only: the explicit statement that the initiative changes hands at 20...Qc7. A player annotating his own game is the strongest kind of evidence about what an idea IS and no evidence at all about whether the move works, which is what the engine is for. The game score was taken from a database and replays legally end to end through blind-chess.html's own move generator.

chessbase-speelman-adams-kasparov-2005.title: Throwback Thursday: Kasparov wins Linares, retires - with Jon Speelman's annotations to Adams-Kasparov
chessbase-speelman-adams-kasparov-2005.author: Jon Speelman (quoted), ChessBase
chessbase-speelman-adams-kasparov-2005.note: GM Speelman's notes as reproduced by ChessBase. Two claims are used: that 22.Be3 was White's best after 21...Kxh7, and that Adams 'seeing no good way to continue his attack, panicked and blundered' with 22.Nb3. Stockfish 18 at depth 22 independently returns Be3 as the best move in that position, which is a rare case of a human annotation and the engine agreeing on a specific move name.

gameknot-adams-kasparov-2005.title: Annotated chess game: Adams - Kasparov, 2005 - Sicilian, Najdorf, English Attack
gameknot-adams-kasparov-2005.author: gameknot user 'tcslick420'
gameknot-adams-kasparov-2005.note: ACCESS CAVEAT: a community annotation by an author of unknown strength, kept for ONE thing - it states the king-safety judgement in words no stronger source states as plainly ('His king may look exposed, but in actuality, there is no immediate danger to his king'). It is corroborated, not relied on: Speelman annotates the same moment and Stockfish 18 scores the position at -2.13 for White. Nothing here rests on this source alone.

keene-reti-capablanca-1924.title: Capa capitulates (annotations to Reti-Capablanca, New York 1924)
keene-reti-capablanca-1924.author: Raymond Keene, The Spectator Australia
keene-reti-capablanca-1924.note: A GM's move-by-move notes to the game that ended Capablanca's eight-year unbeaten run, written around Engqvist's 'Reti: Move by Move'. Used for two explicit judgements: that 18...Ne6 was the move 'fighting more directly for control of the centre', and that Capablanca's queen sorties late in the game were activity rather than an initiative. The score replays legally end to end.

amazingatlas-capablanca-rubinstein-1928.title: The Transformation Doctrine: How Capablanca Won Without Capturing the Weakness
amazingatlas-capablanca-rubinstein-1928.author: Nicholas Van Der Nat (FM), Chess.com
amazingatlas-capablanca-rubinstein-1928.note: A FIDE Master's annotation of Capablanca-Rubinstein, Berlin 1928, whose whole subject is the transformation of one advantage into another at 22.Qxc6. Used for that attribution and for the statement that Rubinstein accepted the isolated d-pawn believing its central control was worth the long-term weakness, which is the static-versus-dynamic bargain named in a game. This blog's printed 'full move order' listings have been found corrupt for several other games in this project, so the score used here comes from a database and was replay-verified; only the prose is taken from the blog.

amazingatlas-capablanca-mattison-1929.title: Game 24: Capablanca vs Mattison, Karlsbad 1929 - Brilliant Smothered Mate
amazingatlas-capablanca-mattison-1929.author: Nicholas Van Der Nat (FM), Chess.com, following Irving Chernev's Logical Chess: Move by Move
amazingatlas-capablanca-mattison-1929.note: Used for the coordination claims: that after 15.Ng5 five White pieces work together toward one goal, and that 16.Bf3 is played to coordinate the two bishops on parallel diagonals before any calculation. Also for the king-safety claim that 15.Ng5 forces ...f5 and permanently weakens the pawn cover. Unusually for this blog, the printed move order for this game replays legally, and it matches the database score.

mcshane-spectator-puzzle-628.title: Puzzle no. 628 - Wade-Korchnoi, Buenos Aires 1960
mcshane-spectator-puzzle-628.author: Luke McShane (GM), The Spectator
mcshane-spectator-puzzle-628.note: A GM's one-line attribution: 'Bob Wade's next move prepared a surprising and decisive breakthrough.' It names the concept for this game's finish without naming the ply, which is why it is used as corroboration rather than as the primary citation for the move.

gelfand-dynamic-decision-making.title: Dynamic Decision Making in Chess
gelfand-dynamic-decision-making.author: Boris Gelfand with Jacob Aagaard
gelfand-dynamic-decision-making.note: ACCESS CAVEAT: consulted through a scanned excerpt of the introduction, not the printed book. The passage used is Gelfand's own statement of the static/dynamic distinction: 'You need to use the momentum to transform it into something valuable ... before it goes away. Essentially it is Steinitz's idea that you have to use your advantage before it disappears. Obviously, this is all about dynamic advantages. With static advantages, the urgency is often much less.' Used to attribute the distinction, not to source any position.

chesstrapguide-kk1985-g16.title: Karpov vs Kasparov 1985 Game 16 PGN: Knight Outpost
chesstrapguide-kk1985-g16.author: Chess Trap Guide
chesstrapguide-kk1985-g16.note: ACCESS CAVEAT: an unattributed training page. Used for one claim, that the d3 knight 'cannot be chased away without damaging White's coordination' and that after 17.Nab1 'White's knights retreat to the back rank, completely uncoordinated'. The page also prints the FEN after 16...Nd3, which matches character for character the FEN this project derives by replaying the database score through its own move generator - so the page corroborates the position even where its analysis is unverified.
